reference.source: Movement-disorder and neurogenetics textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of iron metabolism caused by biallelic variants in CP, encoding caeruloplasmin
Classic triad is diabetes mellitus, retinal degeneration, and adult-onset neurological disease reflecting systemic and cerebral iron overload
Neurological features typically emerge in adulthood and include cognitive decline, cerebellar ataxia, and involuntary movements such as dystonia, chorea, and blepharospasm
Distinctive laboratory profile: absent or very low serum caeruloplasmin with low serum copper but, unlike Wilson disease, high serum ferritin and low serum iron
Iron accumulates not only in the brain but also in the liver, pancreas, and retina, causing the systemic features
MRI with iron-sensitive sequences shows marked iron deposition in the basal ganglia, thalamus, dentate nucleus, and liver
Iron-chelation therapy and other iron-lowering strategies may slow progression, making early recognition worthwhile, in contrast to most other NBIA disorders
Diagnosis rests on the biochemical profile plus imaging and is confirmed by CP molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: Aceruloplasminaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CP, which encodes caeruloplasmin, a ferroxidase that oxidises ferrous to ferric iron to enable iron export and loading onto transferrin. Without functional caeruloplasmin, iron cannot be released normally from cells, so it accumulates within the brain and visceral organs including the pancreas, liver, and retina. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative injury produces neurodegeneration concentrated in the basal ganglia and cerebellum together with diabetes and retinopathy, distinguishing this from copper-overload disorders such as Wilson disease.
additionalDifferentials: Huntington disease and other choreiform disorders
Secondary systemic iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusional iron overload)
additionalInvestigations: Serum caeruloplasmin, copper, iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation showing the characteristic iron-overload-with-low-copper profile
Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences to show basal ganglia, thalamic, dentate, and hepatic iron
CP molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Fasting glucose and HbA1c and ophthalmological/retinal assessment for the systemic features
Assessment of hepatic iron burden where indicated
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline or new psychiatric symptoms
Poorly controlled diabetes with metabolic decompensation
Signs of significant hepatic iron-related dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Untreated, the disorder is progressive with worsening neurological disability, diabetes, and retinopathy, but because iron-lowering therapy can retard progression, prognosis is more favourable with early diagnosis than for most other NBIA subtypes.
pitfalls: Confusing the low serum copper and caeruloplasmin with Wilson disease and giving copper-directed therapy while missing the iron-overload picture
Overlooking the systemic clues of diabetes and retinopathy that point to the diagnosis
Failing to consider a treatable iron-chelation opportunity when NBIA is suspected
Not measuring ferritin, which is characteristically high and helps separate this from copper disorders
management: Iron chelation with deferasirox, deferiprone or deferoxamine to reduce cerebral and visceral iron overload, ideally started early before irreversible neurological damage
Careful haematological monitoring during chelation because of pre-existing microcytic anaemia, adjusting therapy or adding erythropoietin as needed
Fresh frozen plasma or antioxidant supplementation such as vitamin E used as adjuncts to limit ongoing oxidative injury
Standard management of diabetes mellitus and its complications
Symptomatic treatment of dystonia, chorea and parkinsonism, with multidisciplinary support for cerebellar ataxia and cognitive impairment
Ophthalmological monitoring and management of the retinal degeneration
Genetic counselling and testing of relatives given the autosomal recessive inheritance
